title: Some experiments on 3D animated quadruped meshes
author: NatanaelAntonioli
selftext:
I've been working on a workflow for animated quadrupeds using AI-assisted assets. The video below shows my results. Here's what I've managed to do:

1. First, generate the creature with ChatGPT using the same prompt for style consistency.
2. Make it fit a default pose, with straight legs and an open mouth if the attack animation involves biting.
3. Generate the 3D mesh with Meshy 7, then use Remesh > Triangles > Adaptive > High or Ultra.

So far, so good. There may be some issues with symmetry or head tilting, but those are fixable by tweaking the image prompt in GPT or using Photoshop. Blender is also an option if needed.

I've bought a very cheap animal asset pack on Fab. I exported some of the animations as .glb files (Unreal Engine only allows one animation per file, so I wrote a Python script to merge all the animations into one file). Then, I import both the .glb and the mesh I've just generated into Blender.

That's where the trouble begins. I have to match the .glb skeleton to my own mesh by repositioning each bone and deleting any unnecessary ones. If the creature has parts that aren't supposed to deform (like horns), I have to manually edit the weights for each bone.

After that, I just assign the existing animations to my mesh, export it as a .glb, and import it into UE5. It takes some trial and error, and the results aren't great yet, but they seem less goofy than those produced by other alternatives.

3D generators have come a long way since I started working with them. Nowadays, I might have to remove a finger by sculpting in Blender, but I remember having to remove an entire fifth leg from a cow about a year ago. The Remesh feature is also pretty useful and usually fixes smaller mistakes.

How have you folks been doing it?
